• Xylem is a water-conducting tissue of vascular plants which consists of dead hollow cells in the form of fibers and sclereids.

q: Productivity of an ecosystem is composed of which of the following?
options: Net prime productivity and gross prime productivity
solution:
The correct answer is Net primary productivity and gross primary productivity.

Key Points

• Primary production is defined as the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis.

• It is expressed in terms of gm–² yr –¹ or (kcal m–² ) yr –¹ to compare the productivity of different ecosystems

• It can be divided into gross primary productivity (GPP) and net primary productivity (NPP).

• The gross primary productivity of an ecosystem is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis

• Net primary productivity, or NPP, is gross primary productivity excluding the rate of energy loss to metabolism and maintenance.

• Net primary productivity is the rate at which energy is stored as biomass by plants or other primary producers and made available to consumers.

• GPP – R = NPP ( R represents the Respiration losses)

Additional Information

• Primary productivity depends on the plant species inhabiting a particular area.

• Secondary productivity is defined as the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.

• The annual net primary productivity of the whole biosphere is approximately 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter.

• Despite occupying about 70 per cent of the surface, the productivity of the oceans is only 55 billion tons.

q: Which of the following can degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances?
solution:
The correct answer is Fungal enzymes

Key Points:

• Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances. This process is called as catabolism.

• The word catabolism is from New Latin, which got the roots from Greek: κάτω Kato, "downward" and βάλλειν ballein, "to throw".

• It breaks down large molecules like polysaccharides, lipids, etc. into smaller units like monosaccharides, fatty acids, nucleotides, etc.

• It is the breaking-down aspect of metabolism.

• Cells use the monomers released from breaking down polymers to either construct new polymer molecules or degrade them into simple waste products like lactic acid, carbon dioxide, acetic acid, urea, and ammonia, releasing energy.

• The creation of these wastes is usually an oxidation process involving a release of chemical-free energy. Of this, some are lost as heat, and the rest results in the formation of adenosine triphosphate (ATP).​

Additional Information:

• Catabolism is a metabolic process in which complex molecules are broken down into simpler ones with the release of energy. In the context of the given statement, bacterial and fungal enzymes break down the complex detritus into simpler inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide, water, and mineral ions. This breakdown process releases energy that can be used by the decomposers or other organisms in the ecosystem.

• Fragmentation: Detritivores (e.g., earthworms) break down detritus into smaller particles. This process is called fragmentation.

• Leaching: By the process of leaching, water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts.

• Decomposition: It is the process of breaking down a substance into its constituent parts. Decomposition of dead organic matter occurs in nature and it is also called decay or putrefaction.​

q: Which group of animals are named because of their spiny skin and have a peculiar water-driven tube system that they use for moving around?
solution:
The correct answer is Echinodermata.

Key Points

• Invertebrates with pentaradial symmetry, spiny skin, a water circulatory system, and a simple nervous system are known as echinoderms.

• There are around 7,000 extant species in this phylum.

• Echinodermata are only found in the sea.

• Echinoderms include sea stars, sea cucumbers, sea urchins, sand dollars, and brittle stars.

• Echinoderms feature a calcareous endoskeleton with pentaradial symmetry and pigment cells that give them a wide spectrum of hues, as well as cells that contain poisons.

• Water circulates through an echinoderm's water vascular system, which is made up of a central ring of canals that extends along each arm for gaseous exchange and nutrition.

• Echinoderms have two sexes that release their eggs and sperm into the water, where the sperm fertilizes the eggs.ও

• Echinoderms have the ability to reproduce asexually through regeneration.

• The neurological system of echinoderms is exceedingly simple, consisting of a nerve ring in the center and five radial nerves radiating outward along the arms; there is no brain.​

Additional Information

• Phylum Annelida:

• Phylum Annelida contains the class Polychaeta (the polychaetes) and the class Oligochaeta (the earthworms, leeches, and their relatives).

• These species can be found in a variety of settings, including marine, terrestrial, and freshwater, but the presence of water or humidity is essential for their survival, especially in terrestrial habitats.

• This phylum's animals form parasitic and commensal symbioses with other species in their environment.

• Because of its important property of metamerism, or real segmentation, annelids are commonly referred to as "segmented worms" throughout embryonic stages.

• Phylum Arthropoda:

• It includes animals that have been successful in colonizing terrestrial, aquatic, and aerial habitats.

• Arthropods have jointed legs and a chitin exoskeleton.

• Arthropods have a segmented body plan that contains fused segments divided into regions called tagma.

• Arthropods have an open circulatory system and can breathe through their book gills, book lungs, or tracheal tubes.

• Phylum Mollusca:

• Phylum Mollusca is the predominant phylum in marine environments.

• Mollusks have a soft body with a muscular foot, a visceral mass of internal organs, and a mantle, among other features.

• The muscular foot of a mollusk is utilized for mobility and anchoring, and it comes in a variety of shapes and functions, as well as the ability to extend and retract.

• The digestive, nervous, excretory, reproductive, and respiratory systems are all part of the mollusk's visceral mass.

• Most mollusks have a radula, which looks like a tongue but has teeth-like projections for shredding or scraping food.

q: Nutritional care during illness is an organised group of activities which consists of all of the following except:

solution:

• Assessing psychological stress is an important aspect of overall health and well-being, and it can certainly impact a person's nutritional status and food choices.

• However, it may not be considered a part of nutritional care during illness for several reasons.

• Firstly, nutritional care during illness typically focuses on the specific nutritional needs and challenges that arise as a result of the illness itself.

• This includes assessing the impact of the illness on a person's appetite, digestion, and nutrient requirements, as well as identifying any barriers to meeting those needs.

• Secondly, while psychological stress can certainly impact a person's nutritional status, it may be better addressed through other means.

• For example, a person experiencing significant stress or anxiety may benefit from counselling, stress reduction techniques, or other forms of mental health support.

• Lastly, in some cases, addressing nutritional needs may actually help alleviate some of the symptoms of psychological stress.

• For example, certain nutrients, such as omega-3 fatty acids and B vitamins, have been shown to have a positive impact on mood and cognitive function.

q: Name a reproductive strategy in which parasites take advantage of the care of other individuals of the same species or different species to raise their young.
solution:
The correct answer is Brood parasitism. Key Points

• Brood parasitism:-

• It is a reproductive strategy in which a parasite lays its eggs in the nest of another individual of the same species or different species, and the host raises the parasite's young.

• This strategy is often used by birds, such as cuckoos, cowbirds, and honeyguides, but it can also be observed in insects, fish, and mammals.

• Brood parasites have evolved various adaptations to increase their chances of success, such as mimicking the appearance and behavior of the host's eggs or chicks, laying their eggs at the same time as the host, or removing the host's eggs.

• Brood parasitism can have both costs and benefits for the host, depending on the degree of similarity between the parasite and the host, the number of parasites in the host's nest, and the availability of alternative nesting sites.

Additional Information

• Sexual parasitism:-

• It also known as mate parasitism, refers to a reproductive strategy in which a male or female gains access to a mate or a nest by deceiving or coercing the other individual.

• Klepto parasitism, or kleptoparasitism:-

• It​ refers to a feeding strategy in which a parasite steals food from another individual, often by chasing or harassing it.

• Competitive parasitism, or social parasitism:-

• It refers to a reproductive strategy in which a parasite takes over the resources and/or reproduction of a host, often by manipulating its behavior or physiology.

• Along with neutralizing the acid, bile aids in the emulsification of dietary fat, which helps in its digestion.

• It's important to note that excessive bile or reflux of bile into the stomach can cause discomfort and affect the digestive process.​

Additional Information

• Pepsin:

• Pepsin is an enzyme that is released in the stomach to break down proteins into smaller peptides during digestion.

• It is produced by the chief cells in the stomach lining and is activated by the acidic environment of the stomach.

• Pepsin is not involved in making food alkaline, instead, it assists in further breaking down food particles.

• Faulty regulation or overproduction of pepsin can lead to peptic ulcers or other gastric disorders.

• Gastric Juice:

• Gastric juice, a combination of pepsin, hydrochloric acid, and other enzymes, is secreted into the stomach to aid in the digestion of food.

• It is acidic in nature, with a pH ranging from 1.5 to 3.5, which is essential for pepsin's protein digestion process.

• The acidity of gastric juice also kills many bacteria that enter the stomach, providing a protective function against infection.

• Gastric juice is not responsible for making food alkaline, but rather for launching the initial stages of digestion in a highly acidic environment.

• Hydrochloric Acid:

• Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is one of the main components of gastric juice.

• It creates the acidic environment in the stomach needed to activate pepsin and other enzymes.

• HCl helps to break down food and kill ingested pathogens.

• Like pepsin and gastric juice, hydrochloric acid participates in digestion within the stomach, but it does not play a part in making the chyme alkaline.

q: In cells, proteins are synthesised in _.
solution:
The correct answer is Ribosome.

Key Points

• Ribosomes:-

• They are complex molecular machines composed of RNA and protein molecules.

• They exist in all living cells, from bacteria to eukaryotes, and are essential for protein synthesis.

• The primary function of ribosomes is to synthesize proteins through a process called translation.

• They read the genetic information encoded in mRNA (messenger RNA) and use it to assemble amino acids in the correct order to form a protein chain.

Additional Information

• Mitochondria:-

• Mitochondria are double-membraned organelles found in the cells of eukaryotic organisms.

• They have an outer membrane and an inner membrane that encloses the mitochondrial matrix.

• The inner membrane is highly folded into structures called cristae, which increase its surface area for energy production.

• One of the primary functions of mitochondria is to generate energy through aerobic respiration.

• This process involves the conversion of nutrients, particularly glucose, into adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which is the cell's primary energy currency.

• This process occurs in the mitochondria's inner membrane, specifically in the cristae.

• Golgi apparatus:-

• It is also known as the Golgi complex or Golgi body

• It is a membranous organelle found in eukaryotic cells.

• It consists of a series of flattened membrane-bound sacs or cisternae arranged in stacks, along with associated vesicles.

• Nucleus:-

• It is a membrane-bound organelle found in eukaryotic cells.

• It contains the cell's genetic material, including DNA, and serves as the control center of the cell.

• The nucleus is typically spherical and surrounded by a double-layered membrane known as the nuclear envelope.

q: Ferns, horsetails and lycophytes belong to which of the following groups?
solution:
The correct answer is Pteridophyta.

Key Points

• Ferns, horsetails, and lycophytes all belong to the group referred to as Pteridophyta.

• These represent some of the earlier forms of vascular plants on Earth.

• They are classified as a subdivision of the plant kingdom, known as cryptogams, which do not produce seeds or flowers.

• Pteridophyta plants reproduce via spores, which are usually located on the underside of the fronds (leaves) in organs or structures called sporangia.

• The life cycle of Pteridophytes includes two distinct phases – the large, prominent sporophyte and a less visible, but still independent gametophyte also known as a prothallium.

• These plants are typically found in damp, shaded areas, though some have adapted to a variety of other habitats. Ferns, in particular, are known for their feather-like fronds and intricate patterns.

Additional Information

• Bryophyta:

• Bryophyta constitute the group of plants known as mosses and liverworts.

• They often grow in moist, shaded areas and are non-vascular, meaning they lack tissues for transporting water and nutrients.

• Unlike ferns, mosses reproduce using spores but are more primitive, often growing low to the ground.

• Algae:

• Algae is a diverse group of aquatic, photosynthetic organisms.

• They form a crucial part of the food chain in aquatic ecosystems and can range from microscopic sizes (microalgae) to massive kelp.

• Algae is not a homogeneous group but a term used to describe organisms from different evolutionary backgrounds that share some common features.

• Fungi:

• Fungi are a kingdom of usually multicellular eukaryotic organisms which are heterotrophic, meaning they obtain nutrients by consuming organic matter.

• They play a crucial role in nutrient cycling in ecosystems and include yeasts, molds, and mushrooms.

• Some fungi form symbiotic relationships with plants, aiding in nutrient absorption, while others can be pathogenic, causing diseases in plants and animals.

q: Mitochondria is NOT found in .
solution:
The correct answer is bacteria. Key Points

• Mitochondria are not found in bacteria.

• Bacteria are prokaryotic cells and do not contain organelles, such as mitochondria, that are found in eukaryotic cells.

• It's interesting to note that it's widely accepted that mitochondria originated from a type of prokaryote due to a symbiotic event in the distant past, a theory known as endosymbiosis.

Additional Information​​Mitochondria:

• Cell Organelle: Mitochondria are cell organelles in eukaryotic cells. They are not present in prokaryotic cells like bacteria.

• Structure: Each mitochondrion is a double-membrane-bound structure with the outer membrane being smooth and the inner one thrown into folds or cristae.

• Powerhouse of the Cell: Mitochondria are often referred to as the 'powerhouse of the cell'. They are the sites of cellular respiration and produce energy in the form of ATP (adenosine triphosphate).

• Semi-Autonomous: Mitochondria are semi-autonomous organelles. They have their own DNA and ribosomes, meaning they can manufacture their own proteins and replicate independently of the cell in which they reside. This suggests a symbiotic origin to the mitochondria, supporting the endosymbiotic theory.

• Number of Mitochondria: The number of mitochondria in a cell can vary greatly depending on the cell type. For example, cells with high energy needs like muscle cells have more mitochondria, while other cells may have very few.

• Size and Shape: Mitochondria are typically rod-shaped or oval in nature. Their size ranges from 0.5 to 1.0 micrometre in diameter.

• Role in Metabolism: Mitochondria are not only the energy factories of the cell, but also participate in other metabolic tasks such as the synthesis of certain components of blood and hormones, the metabolism of cholesterol, and the regulation of calcium concentration in the cell.

• Cytochromes: Mitochondria contain a number of enzymes, including the cytochromes, which participate in electron transport during aerobic respiration.

• Matrix Space: The space within the inner membrane of a mitochondrion is known as the matrix. It contains a number of enzymes, the mitochondrial DNA, ribosomes, and granules that store calcium phosphate.

• Oxysomes or F1 Particles: The inner membrane of mitochondria bears some spherical bodies called oxysomes or F1 particles. These particles are involved directly in ATP synthesis.

• Krebs Cycle: The process by which energy is produced in the mitochondria, the Krebs (or citric acid) cycle, is a series of biochemical reactions that generate energy through the oxidation of acetate—derived from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins—into carbon dioxide.

• Mitochondrial Disorders: Certain genetic disorders have been linked to mutations in mitochondrial DNA. These include some forms of heart disease, diabetes, and Leigh's syndrome, a progressive neurometabolic disorder.

• Role in Aging: Some theories suggest a role for mitochondria in the aging process. The free-radical theory of aging suggests that accumulated damage from oxidative stress (the imbalance between the production of free radicals and the ability of cells to counteract their harmful effects), largely caused by mitochondria, results in the physiological changes we associate with aging.

• Mitophagy: The process in which defective mitochondria are destroyed by cellular machinery is termed 'mitophagy'. This is a vital process as it assists in maintaining the proper functioning of cells by removing damaged mitochondria that could potentially harm the cell.

• E Gorter and F Grendel made a breakthrough by examining the surface area of lipids and concluded that the lipid surface surrounding cells must be of two layers in the year 1925.

• Their experiment involved extracting lipids from red blood cells and then spreading them out on a water surface to form a monolayer.

• They then measured the area of the monolayer and found that it was twice the area of the surface area of the red blood cells.

• This led them to conclude that the lipid bilayer model of the cell membrane must be correct.

• Gorter and Grendel's work was a major breakthrough in the understanding of cell structure and function.

• It helped to establish the lipid bilayer model of the cell membrane, which is still the accepted model today.
